meaning: Greek/Latin roots about living things and the natural world: bio & vita/viv = life, nat = born, gen = birth or race, carn = flesh, anthrop = human, mort = death, geo = earth, hydro = water, therm = heat, photo = light, path = feeling or disease.
example: Roots unlock new words: (bio) gives biology, (geo) gives geography, (mort) gives mortality.

meaning: Roots about the mind, knowing, trusting and the senses: psych = mind, cogn & sci = know, fid = faith or trust, sens/sent = feel, aud = hear, vid/vis = see, phon = sound, doc = teach, phil & am/amor = love, chron/chrono = time, ann/enn = year, auto = self.
example: The root (psych / cogn / vid-vis) appears in psychology, recognise and vision; (fid) gives fidelity, and (ann/enn) gives annual.

meaning: Roots about carrying, moving, writing and breaking: port, fer and tract = carry or pull, mit/miss = send, vert/vers = turn, pos/pon = place or put, rupt = break, scrib/script and graph/gram = write or draw.
example: The root (port / fer / tract) gives transport, transfer and tractor.

meaning: Prefixes showing how many or how much: mono = one, bi = two, tri = three, semi- = half, multi/poly = many, omni = all, max = greatest, min = small or less, over- = too much, under- = too little, equ = equal.
example: Add the prefix (mono / bi / tri) to get monorail, bicycle and triangle.

meaning: Prefixes that reverse or oppose a meaning: un-, non- and in-/im-/il-/ir- all mean 'not'; anti- means 'against'.
example: Put (un- / non- / in-im-il-ir-) before a word to negate it: unhappy, non-stop, impossible.

meaning: Prefixes showing position or time: pre- and fore- = before or front, post- = after, ex- = out or former, sub- = under or below, inter- = between, intra- = within, trans- = across, tele = far.
example: The prefix (pre- / post- / trans-) fixes time or direction: preview, postwar, transport.

meaning: bene and bene- mean 'good' or 'well'.
example: The root (bene / bene-) gives benefit, benefactor and benevolent.

meaning: Set Latin and formal expressions common in editorial, legal and economic writing.
example: A priori reasoning needs no data; a de facto ruler holds power without the title; income is compared per capita; the report lists, inter alia, three reforms; nota bene, the deadline is fixed; funds are shared pro rata; prima facie the case stands; the status quo remains; vis-a-vis last year growth is slower, and vice versa applies too; the panel was set up on an ad hoc basis.

meaning: Connectors, hedges and time markers that join, limit or soften a statement.
example: The scheme works, (albeit / insofar as / whereby) only in part; henceforth the rule applies, hitherto it did not, and previously it was optional; (conceivably / presumably / ostensibly) it will change; fundamentally the idea is sound; forms may be filed electronically; the erstwhile chairman said nothing.

meaning: deep respect, or showing it. Venerate = to revere deeply (verb); venerable = respected because of age or wisdom; pious = religiously devoted; sacrosanct and inviolable = too sacred or important to be touched or broken.
example: Students (venerate / revere) the venerable teacher; he spoke with (reverence / a reverent tone); the pious crowd treated the shrine as (sacrosanct / inviolable).

meaning: pleasant, warm and easy to get on with. Suave and urbane add smooth social polish; gregarious = fond of company.
example: The host was (affable / amiable / cordial / gregarious); his (suave / urbane) manner put everyone at ease.

meaning: kind, well-meaning and generous in giving. Magnanimity and munificence are the noun forms; altruistic = selflessly caring for others; benign = gentle and harmless; lavish = giving very freely.
example: A (magnanimous / munificent / benevolent / altruistic / lavish) donor funded the school; her (magnanimity / munificence) was widely praised, and the gesture was entirely benign.

meaning: so good that it cannot be faulted or copied. Epitome and quintessential = the perfect example of a type; pristine = spotless or untouched.
example: Her record is (impeccable / inimitable / irresistible); she is the (epitome / quintessential example) of a public servant, and the site remains pristine.

meaning: to build up, back or make stronger; also to copy someone you admire.
example: The reform is (strengthening / emulating) the best global practice; the therapeutic and salubrious effects were clear, and the innocuous change met no resistance.

meaning: to attack someone with harsh words. Castigate, excoriate and vituperate are severe; deride and disparage are mocking or belittling.
example: The court (castigated / excoriated / derided / disparaged / vituperated) the officials for the delay.

meaning: public disgrace, or an act or charge that wounds pride and reputation.
example: He suffered the (ignominy / humiliation / affront) of public dismissal; an (accusation / allegation) followed, and he sued for defamation.

meaning: behaving as if better than everyone else, or plainly ill-mannered.
example: The minister's (haughty / supercilious / imperious / pompous / pretentious) reply angered the house; his (insolent / churlish / obstreperous) aide was worse, and the new recruit was merely gauche.

meaning: excessive false praise given to win favour, or smooth but hollow speech.
example: The court is full of (sycophants / sycophancy); his (glib / unctuous / facile) praise fooled nobody, and the servile staff never disagreed.

meaning: getting worse, shrinking or losing momentum, especially in an economy.
example: Output is (deteriorating / stagnant); the (downturn / recession) deepened, growth hit a plateau, and diminishing returns set in after the devaluation and deindustrialisation.

meaning: to get rid of something completely, or cut it down.
example: The blast (annihilated / demolished / eradicated) the block; the (destruction / elimination) was total, the debris was discarded, and the report was truncated.

meaning: a violent disturbance, a total failure, or the shock that follows one.
example: The policy ended in a (cataclysm / fiasco); the turbulence made markets reel, the poor bore the brunt, and it sounded the knell for the party's old nemesis.

meaning: hostility, armed opposition, open disagreement, or a dangerously tense situation.
example: The (insurgency / belligerence / brinkmanship) put the region on edge; (dissent / disobedience / resistance) spread, dissidents were arrested, and the situation grew (fraught / precarious) amid foreign interference.

meaning: filthy, rotting, brittle or grimly unpleasant.
example: Families live in (squalid / putrid) conditions; the macabre scene shocked inspectors; the brittle pipes and desiccation of the soil worsened malnutrition.

meaning: to stop, forbid, cancel or push something down by force of authority. Note: *sanctioned* is a contronym — it usually means hit with official penalties, but can also mean officially approved; read the context.
example: The order brought (suppression / prohibition) of the protest; the ruling nullified the licence, activists were ostracised and sanctioned, and deportation, extradition and imprisonment followed under a wall of protectionism.

meaning: so strong, fixed or persistent that nothing can overcome, affect or exhaust it.
example: The lead looked (insurmountable / indomitable); he was impervious to criticism, (indefatigable / tenacious) in his work, and the incessant, insatiable demand was sustained for years.

meaning: kept out of sight, held back, or impossible to read or interpret.
example: His (surreptitious / inscrutable / enigmatic) conduct raised doubts; he absconded before the inquiry, staying (aloof / insular) from colleagues, while the case sat dormant at a liminal stage.

meaning: a wrong idea, or the act of getting something wrong or being wrongly named.
example: The claim rests on a (misconception / misnomer / piece of misinformation); the data was (misrepresented / misunderstood), which perplexed readers, and the anomaly proved to be a mere aberration.

meaning: easy to see, notice or single out.
example: The shift was (conspicuous / palpable / pronounced / discernible / salient); the wording was explicit, the finding (notable / distinctive), and each characteristic facet was set out.

meaning: to make something clear, visible, known or pointed out.
example: The chart (elucidates / delineates / demonstrates / indicates / manifests) the trend; the study underscored the risk, the ministry promulgated the rule, and the warning emanated from the data they analysed and observed.

meaning: to work something out, guess it from clues, or turn it over in the mind.
example: Analysts (surmise / postulate / extrapolate) from thin data; the (hypothesis / projection / speculation) is speculative at best, though it derives from real evidence; he dwelt on it for weeks before offering a synthesis.

meaning: showing careful effort, sound judgement, wide learning or calm control.
example: She is (assiduous / erudite / versatile) and known for her discernment; the arduous negotiation demanded (equanimity / sangfroid).

meaning: overly concerned with small details, rules or standards.
example: His (fastidious / pedantic / pernickety) checking slowed the whole process.

meaning: believable, defensible or backed by proof; also being cleared of blame.
example: The claim is (credible / tenable) and the evidence supports it; his fidelity to the facts was total, the inquiry exculpated him, and the exoneration was unanimous.

meaning: not believable, refusing to believe, or breaking trust.
example: The defence is (untenable / purported at best); she was incredulous while a credulous public accepted it; his cynical view proved right when the (perfidious / complicit) aide's perfidy came out.

meaning: convincing argument, formal statements, or speaking mainly to be seen.
example: His case was cogent, the rest pure (grandstanding / performative) talk; the (affirmation / announcement / memorandum) was read out, his insistence grew, and the interrogation produced a litany of querulous complaints despite one important caveat.

meaning: terms about money, markets, trade and the wider economy.
example: A new (levy / default / commodity) shock triggered volatility; overheating followed, firms turned insolvent, and sovereign debt strained the macroeconomic outlook amid globalisation.

meaning: extremely poor, or unwilling to spend. Prodigal is the opposite — wastefully extravagant; rapacious = aggressively greedy.
example: The (indigent / penurious / parsimonious) household had nothing to spare; penury forced the sale, while his prodigal brother squandered a fortune and a rapacious lender took the rest.

meaning: the right to vote and the machinery of elections and representation.
example: Every adult has the (franchise / suffrage); the electorate of each constituency voted in a plebiscite, though delimitation was gerrymandered; registration, participation and grassroots mobilisation decide who the representatives are and how good the representation is.

meaning: the bodies, rules, offices and processes by which a state is run.
example: Good (governance / legislation / regulation) rests on the constitution; parliament debates it, the polity accepts it, and jurisprudence interprets it; impeachment, prosecution and enforcement follow when constitutional limits are broken.

meaning: ideas about who belongs to a nation, who is kept out, and who leads it.
example: Rising (nationalism / xenophobia / antisemitism) hardened attitudes; the diaspora sought asylum, immigration dominated debate, and indigenous claims were ignored as radicalization and partisanship grew.

meaning: people and powers defined by their political stance or dominance.
example: A (conservative / progressive / revolutionary) wing formed; the maverick iconoclast defied the hegemon, the gerontocracy sent an envoy, and the pariah state was frozen out of geopolitical talks.

meaning: working together, giving way, or restoring good relations after trouble.
example: The talks produced (rapprochement / reconciliation); (collaboration / cooperation) replaced hostility, both sides acquiesced and conceded ground, and the new cooperative accommodated every stakeholder.

meaning: to grow, speed up, spread out or push into new ground.
example: Reforms (accelerated / facilitated) growth; the (encroachment / spread) was rapid, cheap credit inundated the market, and the contagious optimism went pandemic.

meaning: creating, installing or expanding physical and industrial capacity.
example: The (construction / development / innovation) drive rebuilt the region; new installations and automation improved connectivity, the yard resumed shipbuilding, and the area was reindustrialised on a firm foundation of infrastructure.

meaning: words marking when something happens or where it falls in an order.
example: At this (juncture) the preliminary stage ended; the prevailing view is that the prospective trajectory is upward, which would be unprecedented; anticipatory planning took precedence over preparation.

meaning: how often or how much something moves or happens.
example: Attacks were (sporadic / occasional); the peripatetic inspector kept moving while the sedentary staff stayed put; each occurrence, appearance and disappearance was logged.

meaning: belonging to something by its very nature, or absolutely required.
example: Risk is (inherent / intrinsic / innate) in the job; trust is (indispensable / requisite) for progress, and openness is a cardinal principle.

meaning: lying next to, linked with, or relying on something else.
example: The two plots are (adjacent / contiguous); the payout is contingent on audit, the dependence on imports is total, and every implication must be factored in.

meaning: something given that becomes part of a larger whole.
example: Each member's (contribution / contributions) mattered; every donor contributing to the fund was named.

meaning: feeling nothing, worn out by too much of something, or the release of pent-up emotion.
example: Voters have grown (apathetic / jaded); the apathy runs deep, and the verdict brought a strange catharsis after months of frustration.

meaning: eagerness, self-belief and the drive to achieve something.
example: Her (enthusiasm / confidence / aspiration / motivation) carried the team; the fascination with the goal never faded, and the target proved attainable.

meaning: physically beautiful, sweet to the ear, or made more attractive.
example: Her (pulchritude / mellifluous voice) drew crowds; the euphony of the hall was perfect, the stage was embellished, and the entertainment and performance were flawless.

meaning: failing in a duty, or acting in a way that damages, pollutes or offends.
example: The (negligence / impunity) was inexcusable; officials contaminated the site, acted (inadvertently / inappropriately), and used profane, unacceptable language that went unacknowledged.

meaning: falling short, being unfairly small, or failing to cope.
example: The team (floundered / was underprepared); we (underestimate / undervalue) the gap; the lopsided deal deepened inequality, and his inexperience, maladroit handling and the resulting unpopularity made him the unfriendliest figure in the room, with only nominal support.

meaning: formally stepping down from a position or right.
example: His (resignation / abdication) ended the crisis.

meaning: to try hard to win or obtain something against others.
example: Firms (vie / compete) for the contract; the bid was strong, and the competition remained fiercely competitive.

meaning: gathering, counting, tracking and studying information.
example: The (survey / sample / data / ratio) showed a clear pattern; the demographic breakdown, traceability of each figure and the examination method were all checked.

meaning: branches of study and the language of science and technology.
example: The (scientific / computational / algorithmic / technological) work spanned neuroscience, anthropology and mythological studies at the university.

meaning: jobs, the people who do them, and the training that leads to them.
example: The (professional / professionals) in each occupation trained through an (apprenticeship / apprenticeships); manufacturers reported strong attendance, and the occupational standard protected their reputation.

meaning: how far something reaches, or how far outside the ordinary it falls.
example: The response was (extraordinary / existential) in scale; the evacuation used all the ammunition and manpower available.

meaning: to gradually become less, smaller or weaker
example: As the crisis passed, public anger began to (abate / ebb / recede / wane / dwindle / diminish).

meaning: to deliberately cut back, limit or reduce something
example: New rules were framed to (curb / curtail / attenuate) wasteful spending; the panel will whittle the list down to five names.

meaning: to make a fear, pain or problem less severe
example: The package was meant to (allay / alleviate / mitigate / ease / dampen) public anxiety.

meaning: to get steadily worse or fall apart
example: Without funding the scheme began to (deteriorate / wither / unravel); thousands languish in overcrowded jails.

meaning: to weaken or damage something, often gradually or secretly
example: Corruption has (eroded / undermined / subverted / crippled / debilitated / enervated) public trust in the institution. Note: subvert = weaken secretly to overthrow; cripple = damage severely.

meaning: to fall fast, steeply or behind
example: Exports (plummeted / plunged / slumped) after the ban; India continues to lag behind its neighbours on this index.

meaning: sense 1: to go down or decrease
example: Enrolment has declined for the third year running.

meaning: sense 2: to politely refuse
example: The minister declined to comment on the report.

meaning: an economic shrinking, fall or standstill
example: Contraction = output shrinking; deflation = a general fall in prices; depreciation = a fall in the value of a currency or asset; depression = a very deep, long collapse; stagnation = a long period with no growth at all.

meaning: weak, easily broken or easily harmed
example: The ceasefire rests on a (feeble / fragile / tenuous) understanding; poor households are the most vulnerable to price shocks.

meaning: lacking energy, effort or life
example: The response was (inert / languid / lethargic / tepid / halfhearted / perfunctory); the once-great mill is now moribund. Note: moribund = about to die out completely.

meaning: a state of tiredness, sluggishness or unwillingness to act
example: A deep (lethargy / lassitude / inertia / malaise) has settled over the bureaucracy. Note: inertia = resistance to change; malaise = a vague sense that something is unwell.

meaning: a fault that spoils something, or to spoil it
example: The riots (marred / dented) the state's image; a single flaw in the design brought the bridge down.

meaning: being emotionally distant; also a small group of troops sent on a separate task
example: He described the tragedy with clinical detachment; a detachment of soldiers was sent to the border.

meaning: rich, or producing wealth
example: They live in an (affluent / opulent) neighbourhood; software turned out to be a lucrative business. Note: opulent stresses visible luxury; lucrative = profit-making.

meaning: the state of being rich and doing well
example: Two decades of reform brought unprecedented prosperity.

meaning: the very rich, and rule by them
example: A steel magnate and two billionaires bankrolled the campaign; critics call the system a plutocracy.

meaning: extremely poor, lacking even food and shelter
example: The floods left thousands destitute.

meaning: careful, non-wasteful management of money and resources
example: A frugal household saves where it can; careful husbandry of water made the district drought-proof.

meaning: to waste money, or greed and corruption over money
example: The board (squandered / frittered away) a decade of profits; profligate spending emptied the treasury; cupidity and venal officials let one clerk embezzle the pension fund. Note: embezzle = steal money you were trusted with.

meaning: money handed out, transferred or set aside
example: Allocate = to set money aside for a purpose; subsidy = government money to lower a cost; bailout = emergency rescue money for a failing firm or bank; largesse = generous giving by the powerful; redistribution = sharing wealth more evenly through tax and welfare; remittance = money sent home by workers abroad; reparations = money paid for war damage.

meaning: debt, what is owed, and available money
example: Arrears = overdue payments; indebtedness = the burden of owing a lot; a creditor is the one owed; leverage = borrowed money used to chase bigger profits; liquidity = how easily assets turn into spendable cash; the state's coffers are its store of funds.

meaning: terms describing economic policy and economic change
example: Fiscal policy covers government spending and taxes, while monetary policy covers money supply and interest rates; neoliberalism favours free markets and trade liberalisation; industrialisation is the shift from a pre-industrial to an industrial economy.

meaning: a rise or return to health after a fall
example: The data point to a (recovery / resurgence) in rural demand.

meaning: the way a person earns a living
example: The ban destroyed the livelihood of thousands of weavers.

meaning: showing off wealth to impress others
example: His ostentatious wedding drew sharp criticism.

meaning: willing to give freely (opposite: stingy)
example: A generous donor funded the entire wing.

meaning: wanting a very large amount; greedy or intensely eager
example: The country has a voracious appetite for imported oil.

meaning: at the very beginning; new and inexperienced
example: The (nascent / fledgling) industry needs protection; the flaw was obvious from the outset.

meaning: to set something off or stir people into action
example: The verdict (sparked / prompted / kindled) protests and (galvanised / mobilised) the opposition; it ushered in a new era and became the catalyst for reform.

meaning: a turning point, model or direction of change
example: 1991 was a watershed year that marked a paradigm shift; the transition to renewables is the clear trend, measured against a 2005 baseline.

meaning: a change made to fix or improve something
example: Parliament may amend the Act; the tax system needs a complete overhaul; adaptation to a warmer climate now requires state intervention.

meaning: changing suddenly and unpredictably
example: Oil prices remain (volatile / unstable); his mercurial temper unsettled the cabinet; instability and the vicissitudes of politics stalled the project.

meaning: refusing to change, or fixed so firmly it cannot be changed
example: Caste privilege is deeply entrenched; a hidebound bureaucracy resists reform and old habits persist; the union stayed (obdurate / obstinate / intransigent / adamant) through eight rounds of talks.

meaning: not following accepted or usual beliefs
example: She defended a heterodox view of growth.

meaning: to keep putting off what must be done
example: The ministry procrastinated for years before acting.

meaning: not final or certain; a first attempt that may change
example: The two sides reached a tentative agreement.

meaning: a chance, or whether something can practically be done
example: Reform opened up new opportunities and raised the possibility of growth; a feasibility study found the plan (feasible / viable).

meaning: aggressive and eager to fight or argue
example: He turned (belligerent / pugnacious / truculent) when questioned.

meaning: open fighting, disagreement or complaint
example: Hostilities resumed along the border; discord within the party grew as the opposition seized on a long-standing grievance.

meaning: great disorder, confusion or violent change
example: The country passed through (turmoil / upheaval) in a (tumultuous / turbulent) decade.

meaning: a humiliating failure or a mockery of the real thing
example: The rollout was a debacle; the inquiry was a travesty of justice.

meaning: a situation where neither side can move forward
example: Talks reached an (impasse / stalemate).

meaning: managing conflict without direct war
example: Diplomacy = managing relations between states through talks; neutrality = refusing to take sides; a proxy is a group fighting on another's behalf; a compromise is a deal where each side gives something up (compromise can also mean to weaken or expose something).

meaning: splitting into rival or separate parts
example: Factional fighting (polarised / cleaved) the party; the polarisation deepened into an open schism, echoing the partition of 1947 and later demands for secession.

meaning: behaving in a weak, servile way to please the powerful
example: Officials kowtow to the minister; his obsequious praise embarrassed everyone.

meaning: pleasure taken in another person's misfortune
example: There was open schadenfreude at the rival firm's collapse.

meaning: skilful, clever and quick
example: She is (adept / adroit / deft / nimble) at handling hostile questions.

meaning: the ability to think and judge quickly and well
example: Her business acumen saved the firm.

meaning: wise and showing good judgement
example: It was a (sagacious / sage / prudent) decision; his nuanced reading of the data impressed the panel. Note: nuanced = alive to fine distinctions.

meaning: careful, thorough and methodical
example: The audit was (meticulous / painstaking / systematic) and the team diligent; every claim was put under close scrutiny.

meaning: in an organised, methodical way
example: Records were systematically destroyed.

meaning: careful about possible danger
example: Investors remain (cautious / wary) about the new rules.

meaning: lacking skill; clumsy and incompetent
example: The rescue effort was hopelessly inept.

meaning: the vocabulary of testing, measuring and reasoning from evidence
example: A heuristic is a rough rule of thumb; an estimate is a careful guess; a variable is a factor that changes and is measured; a control group gets no treatment and is used for comparison; empirical claims rest on observation rather than theory; two things correlate when they move together, and that link is a correlation; results are consistent when they hold from test to test.

meaning: concerning the nature of being and what really exists
example: The debate turned on an ontological question about what a nation is.

meaning: passionate and forceful in support of something
example: He is an (ardent / zealous / vociferous) defender of press freedom. Note: vociferous stresses loudness.

meaning: great energy and enthusiasm for a cause
example: She campaigned with missionary zeal.

meaning: full of energy, movement and strength
example: A (vibrant / kinetic) start-up scene and robust demand lifted the city.

meaning: to give fresh energy to
example: The new coach invigorated a tired side.

meaning: to attract and hold someone's attention completely
example: Her speech captivated the audience.

meaning: hopeful, or calm and happy
example: He stayed sanguine about the outcome; they look back on the halcyon days of the 1990s.

meaning: to discourage or trouble someone, or the pride that invites a fall
example: The scale of the task did not daunt her, though delays continued to vex the team; the collapse was a classic case of hubris.

meaning: genuine and real, not fake
example: The manuscript is (authentic / bona fide).

meaning: faultless; a perfect model of excellence
example: His record is (immaculate / exemplary); she is a paragon of public service and, in her field, incomparable.

meaning: rightful and lawful standing
example: The government's legitimacy was questioned; de jure the office is elected, in practice it is not.

meaning: clear, complete and to the point
example: We need a (coherent / comprehensive) policy; only (germane / pertinent) evidence was admitted.

meaning: not what it appears to be, or hard to pin down
example: The gains proved (illusory / ostensible); a lasting settlement remains elusive.

meaning: abrupt and rude in manner
example: His brusque reply ended the meeting.

meaning: cowardly and lacking courage
example: The pusillanimous response emboldened the attackers.

meaning: the state of not being answerable for one's actions
example: The report blamed official irresponsibility for the lapse.

meaning: worth or note, and public backing
example: The court stressed the importance of the right; the campaign won a celebrity endorsement.

meaning: without meaning to
example: The file was (accidentally / unintentionally) deleted.

meaning: adverbs of manner formed from common editorial adjectives
example: Controversially, the bench went further; the scheme was horrendously mismanaged; progress was excruciatingly slow; architecturally, the building is a landmark.

meaning: public-service terms: waste management, and the right to qualify
example: Sanitation coverage rose sharply; eligibility for the scheme was widened.

meaning: a problem that blocks or delays progress
example: The verdict is a major (hurdle / setback) for the project.

meaning: a difficult, messy or confusing situation
example: The migrants' plight worsened; the government is stuck in a (quagmire / morass / imbroglio / predicament) of its own making and faces the conundrum of how to exit; she rose despite great adversity.

meaning: to struggle with and deal with a difficulty
example: The state must (grapple with / tackle) rising debt and extricate itself from bad contracts.

meaning: a cause of trouble; a drawback
example: Corruption is the bane of the system; the disadvantages of the scheme soon became clear.

meaning: a short break or relief from trouble
example: The rain brought a brief (reprieve / respite) from the heat.

meaning: to throw away or abandon something
example: The party jettisoned the proposal after the backlash.

meaning: to mark out boundaries or limits
example: The order demarcates the forest area.

meaning: alike, simultaneous, or separately distinct
example: The sample was homogeneous; the two trials were concurrent; the syllabus is split into discrete units.

meaning: to place things side by side for comparison
example: The film juxtaposes rural poverty with urban excess.

meaning: real and practical rather than theoretical
example: Voters want tangible results and a pragmatic approach.

meaning: the exact opposite of something
example: His conduct is the (antithesis / converse) of everything the office stands for.

meaning: the quality of being unlike; a disparity
example: The difference between the two states is stark.

meaning: to make something else look small by comparison
example: The new plant dwarfs every rival in the region.

meaning: talking far too much
example: A (garrulous / loquacious) witness held up the hearing.

meaning: high-sounding, inflated and empty in language
example: The speech was (bombastic / grandiloquent / turgid / florid) but said nothing new.

meaning: to catch or arrest someone
example: Police nabbed the suspect at the airport.

meaning: word roots and prefixes that build many editorial words
example: cap/cept = take (capture, accept); ten/tain = hold (retain, contain); duc/duct = lead (conduct, induce); fract/frag = break (fracture, fragment); de- = down or remove (decrease, devalue); vac = empty (vacant, evacuate).

meaning: the highest or most successful point
example: The party was at its (zenith / heyday) in 1984; the protests culminated in a march on the capital.

meaning: the lowest or worst point
example: Relations between the two countries hit their nadir that year.

meaning: useless because it cannot work
example: Further talks would be futile.

meaning: to block, slow down or spoil something so it cannot go forward
example: Bad roads (hamper / hinder / impede / stymie / thwart) relief work; protesters tried to (derail / disrupt) the talks.

meaning: to act in time so that something bad never happens; *deter* = to put someone off by fear of consequences, *obviate* = to remove the need for something
example: Early warning helped (avert / forestall / preclude) a famine; heavy fines (deter) offenders; a good design (obviates) the need for repairs.

meaning: to stop, hold back or bring under control, sometimes by force; *quell / subdue* = put down resistance
example: Troops moved to (halt / stem / quell / subdue) the riot; red tape (stalls / throttles) new projects.

meaning: an official ban, sealing-off or temporary stop on trade, movement or an activity; *interdict* is also used as a verb = to stop officially
example: The council imposed a (blockade / embargo / moratorium) on new mining; patrols (interdict) smuggled goods.

meaning: harsh control that crushes people's freedom; *authoritarian* = a ruler demanding total obedience, *regime* = the ruling government itself
example: Under the (regime), (repression) and the (yoke) of censorship grew; (authoritarianism / totalitarianism) leaves no room for dissent; the army moved to (subjugate) the region.

meaning: easily controlled, over-protected or too relaxed to act; *mollycoddle* is a verb = to pamper
example: A (docile) workforce asks no questions; parents who (mollycoddle) children raise (complacent / indolent) adults.

meaning: unclear, hazy or hard to see through; *obfuscate* is a verb = to make unclear on purpose, *equivocal* = deliberately vague to avoid commitment
example: The reply was (vague / ambiguous / nebulous / equivocal); the accounts stay (opaque / obscure) because officials (obfuscate) the figures.

meaning: hard to handle, hard to solve or impossible to stop
example: The (cumbersome) rulebook makes an (intractable) problem worse; a (wayward / fractious) coalition faced (relentless) pressure.

meaning: to use up, give up or surrender something; *deplete* = to drain a stock, *forfeit* = to lose as a penalty
example: Drought (depletes) reserves; the club had to (forfeit) the match; rebels chose to (cede / capitulate) rather than fight on, and (abandon) their posts.

meaning: a pause, gap or break in an ongoing activity or rule
example: A three-month (hiatus / interregnum) followed the (cancellation) of the session; both sides agreed to a (ceasefire).

meaning: to scold, attack or officially blame someone strongly; *censure* is the most formal, *admonish* the mildest
example: The court (admonished / berated / lambasted / lambaste / slammed / censured / condemned / deplored) the delay; he (harangued) the crowd for an hour.

meaning: abusive speech, or the public disgrace it brings; *denigrate / vilify / malign* are verbs = to run down unfairly, *calumny* = a false damaging statement, *obloquy / opprobrium* = harsh public shaming
example: The campaign was pure (calumny / invective / obloquy / opprobrium), a (tirade) meant to (denigrate / vilify / malign) a rival.

meaning: bitterly harsh in criticism; *indictment* is a noun = a formal charge or a damning verdict on something
example: The (scathing / vitriolic) report followed an (acrimonious) debate and reads as an (indictment) of the whole scheme.

meaning: openly and shockingly bad, deserving blame; *iniquity* is a noun = great wickedness or injustice
example: A (notorious / reprehensible / egregious / flagrant / glaring / heinous) breach of duty exposed the (iniquity) of the system.

meaning: to do with being blamed or cleared of blame; *culpable* = at fault, *absolve / exonerate / vindicate* are verbs = to clear someone
example: Officials were found (culpable) and (accountability) followed; the (onus) and (obligation) lay with the ministry, but the inquiry later (absolved / exonerated / vindicated) the staff.

meaning: rude, ill-mannered or unpleasant in manner; *voluble* = talking non-stop, *obtuse* = slow to understand
example: His (impudent / brazen / boorish / surly / petulant) reply showed him to be (obtuse); a (voluble) speaker filled the rest of the hour.

meaning: a gap, mismatch or difference between things that should match; *lacuna* = a missing part in a law or argument, *outlier* = a value far from the rest
example: The (disparity / discrepancy / gulf / fissure) between the two figures was clear; auditors flagged (deviation), (inconsistencies), a (lacuna) in the rules, a wide (margin) / (margin of error), and one (outlier).

meaning: clashing or likely to cause conflict; *tussle* is a noun = a struggle for control
example: A (disparate / discordant) alliance took up the (contentious) bill, and a long (tussle) followed.

meaning: to openly refuse, reject or strip away; *flout* = to break a rule openly, *disenfranchise* = to take away someone's rights
example: Traders (defy / flout) the ban and (spurn / repudiate) the deal; the new list (disenfranchises) thousands of voters.

meaning: doubt or the inability to settle on an answer; *vacillate* is a verb = to keep changing your mind
example: (Uncertainty) grew as the tests stayed (inconclusive) and the board continued to (vacillate).

meaning: a fine distinction or a fixed point used for comparison; *nuance* = a small but important shade of meaning
example: Every (nuance) matters once a score crosses the (threshold); the scheme became the (benchmark / yardstick) for others.

meaning: a shortfall — of expectation or of money
example: The result was a (disappointment); the budget showed a widening (deficit).

meaning: prefixes meaning 'opposite / away' (dis-) and 'wrong / badly' (mis-)
example: (dis-) gives disagree, dishonest, disappear; (mis-) gives misunderstand, misguide, misuse.

meaning: a coming-together, a deal, or the process of reaching one; *ratification* = the formal approval that makes a deal binding
example: After long (negotiation / parley) at the (conference), the (coalition) reached an (accord) by (consensus); the (combination / convergence / cohesion) of views survived (ratification).

meaning: to bring or come together, or to settle differences; *mediate* = help two sides agree, *arbitrate* = decide as a neutral judge
example: The factions (coalesce / converge) once talks (reconcile) their demands; the panel was (convened) to (mediate / arbitrate) the dispute.

meaning: to follow, agree to, or bring someone round; *compliance* is a noun = the act of obeying, *stipulate* = to set a condition
example: Firms must (abide) by and (adhere) to the code, and (compliance) is checked; the state (acceded) to the demand after leaders (persuaded / co-opted) the rebels, and the pact (stipulates) an annual review.

meaning: united, matching, or added together; *unilateral* = done alone, *multilateral* = by many together
example: A (cohesive / compatible) team took the (multilateral) route rather than a (unilateral) one; the (aggregate / cumulative) effect of (incremental) steps was large.

meaning: prefixes meaning 'with / together' (co-, con-) and 'one' (uni-)
example: (co-/con-) gives cooperate, connect, coexist; (co/con) gives collaborate, contract; (uni) gives unite, unique, universe.

meaning: harmful, threatening or deeply unpleasant; *noxious* = poisonous, *ominous / baleful* = warning of coming evil, *lachrymose* = tearful
example: (Adverse / detrimental / deleterious / noxious) fumes filled the street; the (baleful / ominous / grim) forecast made for a (harrowing), (lachrymose) night.

meaning: harmful in a hidden, spiteful or scheming way; *insidiously* is the adverb, *machinations* a noun = secret harmful plotting
example: (Insidious / pernicious / malignant) rumours spread (insidiously); (malevolent / vindictive) rivals and their (machinations) did the rest.

meaning: extremely harsh, blunt or inflaming
example: The (draconian) order and its (stark) wording were (incendiary); (wanton) destruction followed, with a (galvanic) effect on protesters.

meaning: a settled or low-grade bad condition; *endemic* = always present in a place or group, *subprime* = high-risk and poor quality
example: Corruption is (endemic) here; (subprime) lending and (ineffective) oversight caused the crash.

meaning: an unpleasant clash of sound, or acute discomfort
example: A (cacophony) of horns drowned the speech, adding to the government's (embarrassments).

meaning: prefix meaning 'bad' or 'badly'
example: (mal-) gives malfunction, malnutrition, maltreat.

meaning: certain, unstoppable or beyond doubt; *inexorable* stresses that nothing can halt it
example: Defeat looked (inevitable / ineluctable / inexorable); the evidence was (indubitable / unequivocal).

meaning: words that link a conclusion to its reason, or state it without doubt
example: The data is clear; (ergo / hence / thus / thereby) the policy fails, and the panel (unequivocally) rejected it.

meaning: authority, its scope, or its source; *paramount / predominant* are adjectives = above all others, *incumbent* = the current office-holder or a binding duty
example: Safety is (paramount) and the (predominant) concern; the (incumbent) claims a (mandate) within the (remit) of the (legislative) branch, which in a (democracy) rests on (sovereignty) and regional (autonomy); (privatisation) was approved.

meaning: to cause or produce something, or to name the cause; *causation / factor* are nouns = the causal link and a contributing cause
example: Delay (engenders / breeds) anger and (inflicts / wreaks) real damage; analysts (attribute) this to one (factor), though (causation) is unproven.

meaning: what follows from an event; *corollary* = something that logically follows, *repercussion / fallout* = the indirect bad after-effects
example: In the (aftermath), the (fallout / repercussions / ramifications) were severe; the (outcome) was a natural (corollary) of the decision.

meaning: to depend on, require, or balance out
example: Success (hinges) on funding, which (entails) new taxes; savings elsewhere (offset) the cost.

meaning: to seize power or territory by force, or to throw someone out of it; *annexation / coup / insurrection* are nouns naming such acts
example: Generals (deposed / ousted) the president and (usurped / wrested) control in a (coup); the (insurrection) let them (annex) the border district, an (annexation) no one recognised.

meaning: revenge, or the cancelling / risking of something; *jeopardise* = to put at risk, *abrogate / annul* = to cancel officially
example: Fear of (reprisal / retaliation) grew; the strike would (jeopardise) the truce, and parliament moved to (abrogate / annul) the treaty.

meaning: to make a bad situation worse
example: Fresh curbs only (aggravate / exacerbate) the shortage.

meaning: governed by chance rather than plan; *hapless* = unlucky and helpless, *fortuitous* = luckily unplanned
example: The (hapless) crew survived by a (fortuitous), (random) turn of the tide.

meaning: power or influence and the ability to use it; *wield* is a verb = to hold and use power, *propensity* = a natural tendency
example: A bloc with real (clout) exercises (hegemony) and (wields) it freely, given the (capacity) to act and a (propensity) to intervene.

meaning: instruments or roles used to manage a situation; *palliative* = a stop-gap that relieves but does not cure
example: An (interlocutor) was appointed; the relief package was a mere (palliative), and the (tariff) stayed in place.

meaning: to think, work out or perceive; *deliberate* also = done on purpose (adj.), *anticipation / experience* are nouns for expecting and for what you have lived through
example: The board will (mull / deliberate) the plan and (reckon) the cost; from the data you can (infer / discern) a trend; (anticipation) ran high, and (experience) shaped the verdict.

meaning: to give as a reason or justify it; *simulation* is a noun = a modelled run used to predict behaviour
example: Officials (cite) new data that (warrants) a review, backed by a computer (simulation).

meaning: Latin roots: flect/flex = bend, flu/flux = flow, ject = throw, spec/spect = see or look
example: (flect/flex) gives reflect, flexible; (flu/flux) gives fluent, influx; (ject) gives reject, eject; (spec/spect) gives inspect, spectator.

meaning: to examine, measure or establish something; *probe* is also a noun = an investigation
example: Auditors (scrutinise / investigate / probe) the accounts to (assess / gauge / ascertain) the loss and (quantify) it.

meaning: to express sorrow or regret; *contrite / penitent* are adjectives = feeling deep remorse for a wrong
example: Leaders (lament / bemoan) the loss; the (contrite / penitent) official offered to resign.

meaning: giving a vaccine to protect against a disease
example: A mass (vaccination) drive covered every district.

meaning: equal to or the same as something (usually something bad)
example: Silence here is (tantamount) to consent.

meaning: to praise someone or something publicly
example: Critics (lauded / hailed / eulogised / acclaimed) the new welfare scheme.

meaning: strong public praise and approval
example: The reform won wide (acclaim / approbation) from economists.

meaning: deserving praise, or justified by the facts
example: The effort was (laudable / warranted) given the scale of the crisis.

meaning: to publicly support, approve or adopt a cause or agreement; *ratify* = formal approval of a treaty
example: The party (endorsed / espoused / advocated) the new labour code; Parliament finally ratified the treaty.

meaning: a loyal, reliable supporter of a cause
example: She has been a lifelong (advocate / stalwart) of press freedom.

meaning: to support, strengthen or encourage the growth of something; *underpin* = form the base of; *embolden* = give courage
example: The subsidy (bolstered / boosted / augmented / fostered) rural demand; strong institutions underpin democracy; the win emboldened the protesters.

meaning: something that pushes an activity forward or encourages action
example: The tax cut gave a much-needed (boost / impetus / stimulus / incentive) to manufacturing.

meaning: the main supporting part on which something rests; *collateral* = the asset pledged to back a loan
example: Small farms are the (backbone / keystone) of the rural economy; the loan required land as collateral.

meaning: firmly loyal, unwavering and able to withstand difficulty
example: He remained a (staunch / steadfast / stalwart) defender of the constitution; the economy proved resilient.

meaning: the ability to recover quickly after a shock or disaster
example: The community showed remarkable resilience after the floods.

meaning: to grow well and become very successful
example: Start-ups thrive where regulation is light.

meaning: to win over or gather support, votes or attention
example: The party (wooed / garnered) young voters ahead of the polls.

meaning: a serious, formal promise; to promise firmly
example: The government (pledged / vowed) to double spending on health; the two states signed a covenant on water sharing.

meaning: a serious effort to achieve something
example: The mission was a bold scientific endeavour.

meaning: the process of bringing something back to its original state
example: The restoration of the old fort took five years.

meaning: to get back money or losses
example: Airlines struggled to recoup pandemic losses.

meaning: to prove or back up a claim with evidence
example: Independent data (corroborated / substantiated / verified) the whistleblower's account.

meaning: to help someone do something wrong
example: Officials were accused of aiding and abetting illegal sand mining.

meaning: to give someone the right to vote or full citizenship rights
example: The amendment enfranchised millions of young voters.

meaning: based on equal treatment or on rising by talent rather than birth
example: He pushed an egalitarian tax policy; the exam system is meant to be a meritocracy.

meaning: extremely serious, severe or hard to bear; *stringent* = strict; *onerous/gruelling* = heavy and exhausting
example: The report warned of a (dire / acute) water shortage; the government took drastic steps and imposed stringent rules; the onerous, gruelling paperwork deterred applicants.

meaning: frighteningly difficult, or about to happen very soon
example: The task was daunting, with an (imminent / looming) deadline.

meaning: to appear close and threatening; to be about to happen
example: A fresh crisis looms over the sector.

meaning: to make a bad situation worse or grow more serious over time
example: Delays (compounded / escalated) the crisis; the grievance was left to fester.

meaning: a rise in the intensity of a conflict or dispute
example: Both sides warned against further escalation along the border.

meaning: expressed with strong, forceful feeling or conviction; *trenchant* = sharp and cutting; *compelling* = very convincing
example: She made a (fervent / vehement / emphatic) appeal for calm; his trenchant, compelling critique changed the debate.

meaning: a person holding extreme, uncompromising views; *demagogue* = a leader who stirs emotion rather than facts
example: The party was captured by (zealots / hardliners); the campaign was led by a demagogue.

meaning: political styles based on aggressive nationalism, mass appeal, one-man rule, or favour-trading
example: The speech slid into jingoism; critics saw populism, clientelism and creeping autocracy in the new order.

meaning: strict economic policy with sharply reduced public spending
example: Years of austerity hollowed out public services.

meaning: severe, widespread lack of food causing hunger and death
example: Drought pushed the region towards (famine / starvation).

meaning: a strong, angry public reaction against something
example: The order triggered a fierce backlash from farmers.

meaning: a penalty imposed on a country; or, oppositely, official permission
example: The council imposed sanctions on the regime; the ministry sanctioned the new post.

meaning: to accuse someone of wrongdoing; *indict* = formally charge
example: The agency (indicted / blamed) the contractor and alleged large-scale fraud.

meaning: the breaking of a rule, law or promise
example: The order was a clear breach of privacy law.

meaning: the act of impairing integrity or moral principle; dishonest use of power
example: Corruption in procurement drained the budget.

meaning: a punishment or fate that is justly deserved
example: The scam's masterminds finally got their comeuppance.

meaning: to force, push or deliberately drive someone into acting; *goad/provoke* = to needle into a reaction
example: Officials (coerced / compelled) traders to comply; the remarks (goaded / provoked) the crowd.

meaning: to request strongly and earnestly
example: Doctors (implored / urged) the public to stay indoors.

meaning: an urgent and emotional request
example: The court heard a plea for immediate relief.

meaning: affecting a whole system, not just one part; built into how things work
example: The audit exposed systemic failures in the supply chain.

meaning: large or important enough to matter, especially in results
example: The trial showed a significant drop in infections.

meaning: lack of seriousness; treating a serious matter lightly
example: There is no room for levity in a public health crisis; the court dismissed the frivolous petition.

meaning: to rise, grow or spread quickly; *wax* = to increase gradually
example: Prices (escalated / soared / surged) after the ban; misinformation proliferated online while the party's influence waxed.

meaning: a sudden or sustained increase in level, price or power
example: A (surge / hike) in fuel rates followed; the decade saw rapid expansion and the ascendancy of a new elite.

meaning: to raise a price or rate
example: The bank hiked interest rates again.

meaning: the general rise in prices over time
example: Food inflation stayed above eight per cent.

meaning: to spread something widely; *diffuse* also = to calm a tense situation
example: The app (disseminated / diffused) weather alerts to millions; talks helped diffuse the tension.

meaning: very common and spreading everywhere, usually of something bad; *ubiquitous* = present everywhere
example: Corruption was (rampant / rife) in the department; smartphones are now ubiquitous.

meaning: how common or widespread something is
example: The survey measured the prevalence of anaemia among children.

meaning: more and more over time
example: Cities are increasingly reliant on tanker water.

meaning: to begin to grow or develop, like a seed or an idea; *germinal* = at the earliest stage
example: The idea germinated in a college seminar; the paper is the germinal work in the field.

meaning: to produce or give a result or amount
example: The new seed yields twice as much per hectare.

meaning: a large number of people leaving a place
example: The lockdown triggered an exodus of migrant workers.

meaning: to push a group to the edges of society and ignore their needs
example: The policy further marginalised landless labourers.

meaning: the size or scale of something; to find out that size
example: No one grasped the magnitude of the loss; the study measured its true cost.

meaning: root MAGN = great, large
example: magnify, magnificent, magnitude, magnate.

meaning: prefix SUPER-/SUR- = above, over
example: superman, supervise, surplus, surface.

meaning: prefix RE- = again, back
example: rewrite, return, rebuild, revise.

meaning: root CIRCUM = around
example: circumference, circumnavigate, circumspect.

meaning: root DICT = say, speak
example: dictate, predict, contradict, verdict.

meaning: root CRED = believe
example: credit, credible, incredible, credentials.

meaning: root MAL = bad
example: malice, malevolent, malfunction, malign.

meaning: able to continue long-term; taking the whole into account rather than parts
example: The plan is neither (sustainable / holistic) nor affordable.

meaning: existing in large, more-than-enough quantities
example: The region has (abundant / ample / copious / profuse) rainfall.

meaning: to exist in large numbers; to be plentiful
example: Rumours abound about a cabinet reshuffle.

meaning: a very large number or an excess of something
example: The scheme drew a (plethora / surfeit / myriad) of complaints.

meaning: more than is needed; unnecessary
example: The clause was (superfluous / redundant) and was dropped.

meaning: the extra amount left when income is more than spending
example: The state recorded a revenue surplus this year.

meaning: far too high or large in price, amount or weight
example: Patients were charged (exorbitant / hefty) fees.

meaning: large in size or amount
example: A substantial share of the budget went unspent.

meaning: a serious shortage or very small amount of something
example: There is a (dearth / paucity) of reliable district-level data.

meaning: not enough; very small in amount
example: The diet was (deficient / meagre); the gains were marginal.

meaning: the typical middle value; close to but not exactly correct
example: The average yield was about four tonnes, an approximate figure at best.

meaning: using very few words; short and clear
example: His reply was (concise / laconic).

meaning: extreme greed for wealth
example: Corporate avarice drove the collapse.

meaning: to destroy a large part of something; stronger than *reduce*
example: The drought decimated the cattle herd.

meaning: not controlled or held back; without limits
example: (Unbridled / Unfettered) construction choked the wetland.

meaning: to stop something from developing or being expressed
example: The law stifles dissent.

meaning: a supposed cure for all problems (usually said it is NOT one)
example: Technology is no panacea for rural poverty.

meaning: to put forward a claim or idea as true so it can be debated or tested
example: The authors (contend / posit) that growth alone will not cut inequality.

meaning: to say something again for emphasis
example: The minister reiterated that no tax would rise.

meaning: clear, fluent and easy to follow; *eloquent* stresses persuasive skill
example: Her (eloquent / lucid / limpid / pellucid) explanation won the house over.

meaning: public argument and discussion on a topic; *rhetoric* often implies empty persuasive language
example: The campaign was heavy on rhetoric; the public discourse and its dialectic of opposing views produced little.

meaning: believable and reasonable enough to be true
example: The explanation is plausible but unproven.

meaning: as can reasonably be claimed, or as claimed by others without proof
example: It is arguably the biggest reform in a decade; the funds were purportedly spent on training.

meaning: in spite of; and *per se* = in itself, taken on its own
example: Notwithstanding the delays, work continued; the rule is not unfair per se.

meaning: limited, temporary or not final; *qualified* support = support with conditions
example: The party gave (qualified / provisional) backing; the ordinance is only a stopgap.

meaning: the set of methods used to carry out research
example: The paper's methodology was criticised by statisticians.

meaning: to repeat a study or test to check the result holds
example: No team could replicate the original finding.

meaning: about how things should be, based on rules or values, not just how they are
example: The report makes a normative case for free school meals.

meaning: to confuse a result by mixing in a hidden cause
example: Income differences confounded the study's conclusions.

meaning: a self-contradictory statement, or a sharp split into two opposed parts
example: It is a paradox that food-surplus states report hunger; the growth-versus-environment dichotomy dominates the debate.

meaning: a difficult situation where it is hard to decide what to do
example: The board faced a quandary over the merger.

meaning: a calculated move or secret scheme made to gain advantage
example: The walkout was a political gambit; the machinations of the lobby were later exposed.

meaning: honest, direct and truthful in what one says
example: She gave a (candid / forthright / veracious) account of the failures.

meaning: truthfulness; accuracy (root VER = truth)
example: The court questioned the veracity of the affidavit.

meaning: fair and just to all
example: The panel urged a more equitable sharing of river water.

meaning: deeply religious or sincerely committed
example: He was a devout follower of the movement.

meaning: to correct or set right a wrong
example: The tribunal exists to (redress / rectify) such grievances.

meaning: to cancel or take back an order or decision
example: The ministry rescinded the circular within a week.

meaning: to send someone back to their own country
example: Hundreds of workers were repatriated after the war.

meaning: not strict; patient and self-controlled in the face of provocation
example: The judge was lenient; the state showed unusual forbearance.

meaning: action taken to make a problem less serious
example: Flood mitigation works were funded this year.

meaning: one-sided and splitting people into hostile camps
example: The bill was (partisan / divisive) from the start.

meaning: putting on a false show - of moral superiority, of emotion, or of grandeur
example: The speech was (sanctimonious / histrionic / grandiose) and short on detail.

meaning: understanding a situation only after it has happened
example: In hindsight, the warning signs were obvious.

meaning: done secretly to avoid notice, often something illicit
example: The (clandestine / furtive) meetings were caught on camera.

meaning: mysterious, obscure and understood by only a few
example: The rules are (arcane / cryptic / esoteric / recondite / abstruse) even to lawyers.

meaning: existing but not yet visible or active; lying beneath the surface
example: The (latent / underlying) causes of the unrest went unaddressed.

meaning: understood or implied without being said directly
example: There was (tacit / implicit) approval from the top.

meaning: to reveal secret information
example: The officer refused to divulge the source.

meaning: deliberately making something confusing to hide the truth
example: The reply was pure obfuscation.

meaning: to hide or play down something bad so it seems less serious
example: The report (glossed over / belied) the true scale of the losses.

meaning: a thin, often false, outer appearance
example: Beneath the veneer of order lay deep dysfunction.

meaning: letting light through; open and easy to see into (opposite of opaque)
example: The process must be transparent and auditable.

meaning: strong bitter hostility and resentment between people
example: The talks collapsed amid (animosity / acrimony / rancour).

meaning: showing strong enmity or doing active harm; *vituperative* = bitterly abusive in words
example: The climate was (hostile / inimical) to investment; his (virulent / vituperative) attacks drew censure.

meaning: stubbornly refusing to obey or to be calmed
example: The (recalcitrant / implacable) faction blocked every compromise.

meaning: behaving without moral restraint
example: The court described his (dissolute / licentious) conduct.

meaning: impossible to remove or erase
example: The riots left an indelible mark on the city.

meaning: extremely complicated and confusing, like a maze
example: The subsidy rules are labyrinthine.

meaning: to build or create a bond; or, in the other sense, to fake a document
example: The two states forged a water-sharing pact; he was jailed for forging signatures.

meaning: lasting only a very short time
example: The gains proved (ephemeral / transient).

meaning: coming later than it should
example: A belated apology was issued.

meaning: sudden and unexpected
example: The scheme came to an abrupt end.

meaning: a sign of something to come
example: The rains were a harbinger of a good harvest.

meaning: a quiet or calm period
example: There was a brief lull in the fighting.

meaning: gloomy and without hope; *despondent* describes a person's low mood
example: The outlook was (bleak / dismal); relatives looked (despondent / lugubrious) outside the hospital.

meaning: to make someone lose hope or trust
example: Voters were disenchanted by the broken promises.

meaning: cheerful and in high spirits; *buoyant* also = economically strong
example: The crowd was (jubilant / jovial); the host was genial and markets stayed buoyant.

meaning: to calm or soothe someone who is angry or upset
example: The package was meant to (assuage / mollify / placate) the protesters.

meaning: calm and unbothered, showing little emotion or concern
example: He remained (phlegmatic / nonchalant) through the crisis.

meaning: unrealistic and impractical in a hopeful, idealistic way
example: It was a quixotic bid for the presidency.

meaning: to make a bad situation better
example: The grant helped ameliorate rural distress.

meaning: to mislead by hiding the truth; *beguile* also = to charm; *prevaricate* = to dodge rather than lie outright
example: He set out to (deceive / dissemble / beguile) investors; the witness prevaricated for an hour.

meaning: to make up something false
example: The dossier was entirely fabricated.

meaning: false or dishonest; *specious* = looks correct but is actually false; *duplicitous* = two-faced
example: The (mendacious / duplicitous) testimony rested on (spurious / specious) claims.

meaning: doubtful and possibly not honest or true
example: The firm has a dubious record on safety.

meaning: clever trickery used to deceive
example: The deal was pushed through by legal chicanery.

meaning: holding back - through shyness, unwillingness, or careful caution
example: He was (diffident / reticent / reluctant) about speaking; the ministry stayed circumspect on the figures.

meaning: habitually saying very little
example: The taciturn official gave one-word answers.

meaning: eager, or sharply aware and perceptive
example: She was keen to start, and had a keen eye for detail.

meaning: clever and shrewd, with sharp insight
example: It was an (astute / perspicacious) reading of the market.

meaning: very bold and fearless, sometimes shockingly so
example: It was an (audacious / intrepid) rescue attempt.

meaning: acting fast without thinking; rushing in recklessly
example: The impetuous decision was made headlong, without consulting anyone.

meaning: extent to which something is affordable, as measured by its cost relative to the amount that the purchaser is able to pay
example: First-time home buyers are feeling the squeeze of higher interest rates with mortgage affordability at its worst level for 16 years.
